title: This week in India's growth story: November 9-15, 2026
excerpt: A week of 15 stories: a port that broke its own cargo record twice in a month, UPI crossing Rs 1 lakh crore in average daily value for the first time, a 23% export surge, and a run of history that stretched from a Sikh empire builder to the scientist who gave India its first tissue-studying institute - alongside the diaspora figures carrying India's name into new legislatures and executive suites abroad.
bodyHtml:
Fifteen stories this week, across a stretch that leaned harder into history than any week before it - five separate On This Day profiles, from an empire-builder to a 19-year-old revolutionary - while the sector numbers kept doing what they've done all year: breaking records that were themselves set only weeks earlier. Here's the week, day by day.

Monday, November 9

Uttarakhand marked its Foundation Day, carved out of Uttar Pradesh in 2000 and renamed from Uttaranchal in 2007. Nithya Raman, born in Kerala, became LA's Mayor-elect after defeating incumbent Karen Bass. India's Services PMI hit 55.8 in October, a four-month high. And in Sheohar, Bihar, Geeta Devi built Sagar Ice Cream into a livelihood from nothing.

Tuesday, November 10

Surendranath Banerjee, dismissed from the Indian Civil Service on a technicality in 1874, went on to found the Indian Association and lead it into the Indian National Congress. Jyot Singh, raised by Sikh and Punjabi immigrant parents in Norcross, Georgia, became the first Sikh American elected to the Georgia General Assembly. And India's merchandise exports jumped 23.04% year-on-year to $44.40 billion in September.

Wednesday, November 11

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, born in 1888, became Congress's youngest-ever president at 35 and later served as independent India's first Education Minister for over a decade - honoured every year since as National Education Day. A month after crossing 800 million transactions a day, UPI broke its own record again: 25.47 billion transactions in October, with average daily value crossing Rs 1 lakh crore for the first time ever.

Thursday, November 12

Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, who founded Banaras Hindu University and served as its vice-chancellor until 1938, was posthumously awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2014 - 68 years after his death. And Deendayal Port in Kandla, Gujarat, crossed 100 million tonnes of cargo 51 days faster than its own previous fastest pace, after setting a new all-India single-day cargo record just weeks earlier.

Friday, November 13

Maharaja Ranjit Singh, born in 1780, inherited a small Sikh chiefdom at age 12 and built it into an empire stretching from the Khyber Pass to Tibet - running one of the most stable, pluralistic powers of its era for a 40-year reign.

Saturday, November 14

Birbal Sahni, born in 1891, became India's foremost palaeobotanist and founded the Institute of Palaeobotany in Lucknow in 1946 - still running today as an autonomous government research body. And Rahul Goyal, born and educated in India with a mechanical engineering degree from Mysore University, became President and CEO of Molson Coors, one of the world's largest brewers.

Sunday, November 15

Birsa Munda, born in 1875 in present-day Jharkhand, led a tribal uprising that forced through the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, still protecting tribal land rights today - his birthday now marked nationally as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

Fifteen stories, one week. A port that keeps beating its own records, a payments system that treats every milestone as a floor, and a run of history stretching from an 18th-century empire-builder to a 20th-century scientist - each one still shaping the India that followed them.

coverHeadlines: India's services sector just hit a 4-month high. And input costs just hit a 6-year low.
India's exports just jumped 23% in a single month - against the same month last year.
A month after crossing 800 million transactions a day, UPI just broke its own record again. This time, the average day crossed Rs 1 lakh crore.
A Gujarat port just broke its own fastest-ever record. By breaking it even faster than before.
A 12-year-old inherited a small chiefdom. By the time he was done, he ruled an empire that stretched from Kabul to Tibet.
He spent his life reading the story written in stone - fossilized plants that proved India's past stretched back hundreds of millions of years.
He led a tribal uprising against colonial exploitation. India now marks his birthday as a national day of pride.
